newsitem.title: JAPAN: Moody's cuts rating outlook of four Japanese banks.
newsitem.headline: Moody's cuts rating outlook of four Japanese banks.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service said on Monday that it had lowered its ratings outlook for Nippon Credit Bank Ltd, Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd, Yasuda Trust & Banking Co Ltd and Chuo Trust & Banking Co Ltd to negative from stable.

It said the change reflected its view that Japanese policy on resolution of the issue of distressed institutions was shifting from one of protection and forbearance to resolution via liquidation, which could expose creditors to risk.

It said the downgraded banks had been having serious asset quality problems and their respective earnings, existing capital and reserves might not provide a sufficient cushion to absorb required loan-loss provisions.
The weak financial fundamentals of these banks were reflected in their "E" bank financial-strength ratings -- Moody's lowest.

Moody's said it had maintained the banks' ratings on long-term deposits, short-term deposits and senior unsecured bonds at the investment-grade level, based on its assumption that regulatory authorities would remain committed to preventing a failure among Japan's 20 major banks.

But due to a change in the Japanese government's stance, the implicit regulatory support for financial institutions would likely decrease while the associated credit risk would increase over the medium term, it said.
It said that the E-rated Japanese banks would not be able to resolve their asset-quality problems using only their own resources in the near term.

It said that because of an accelerating trend toward deregulation, pressure on their franchises was increasing as well because regulatory barriers between different forms of banking were likely to disappear or diminish dramatically over the medium term.
With clearer regulatory guidelines to be offered under a new deposit resolution framework, these weaker institutions may face constraints on their customary operations, Moody's said.
Should the banks ultimately fail, certain classes of creditors may eventually be exposed to loss, it said.

Moody's said that the recent volatility in the Japanese stock market had had only a limited immediate impact on the banks' capital adequacy ratios so far. But a sustained decline in stock prices could result in accounting losses that could ultimately erode their core capital, it said.
As regulators will concentrate on capital ratios to a greater extent, the weaker core capital at these institutions would mean they would be under heightened regulatory scrutiny, Moody's said.
